Amid weaker economic tailwinds, higher capital costs, geopolitical barriers, and AI disruption, BCG argues that CEOs need a tailored “growth compass”: a system for choosing, combining, and continually recalibrating the growth bets most likely to create shareholder value.

Growth matters most when it creates value, not simply revenueRevenue growth drove 49% of ten-year shareholder returns among top-quartile S&P 500 performers, yet only 60% of companies achieved value-creating growth—making disciplined choices essential.

Companies should combine growth paths rather than pursue isolated betsCEOs can blend six vectors, from strengthening commercial execution to acquisitions, around shared advantages. Trane, for example, achieved 23% annualized five-year shareholder returns by pairing AI-enabled capabilities with cooling-market expansion.

Execution requires enterprise-wide ownership and resilienceThe CEO must own the compass, while finance enforces investment discipline and business leaders execute. Integrating functions, shared data, and risk planning prevents promising opportunities from competing for scarce resources.

AI makes continual recalibration a strategic necessityAI changes the cost and speed of expansion while empowering new competitors. Among AI-adoption leaders, 6% of surveyed US public companies, growth—not cost cutting—was the main source of value creation.

Charting a course to robust, sustainable growth demands more of CEOs than ever before. With macroeconomic tailwinds weakening, capital costs rising, geopolitical barriers mounting, and AI reshaping competition, today’s leaders must fight harder for growth—and on more than one front.The challenge for CEOs is deciding which fights are worth the effort. The forces reshaping competition may be widespread, but their impact varies sharply across and even within industries. Inflation, for example, squeezes consumer spending while creating openings for value-oriented brands. Geopolitical shifts can disrupt global supply chains while benefiting domestic manufacturers. And AI can undermine long-established business models while giving scrappy upstarts a foothold they might once have struggled to gain.CEOs cannot control these forces, but with the right Growth Compass, they can identify where they have the greatest opportunity to win and focus their investments accordingly.

How CEOs Can Build and Recalibrate Their Growth Compass

The broad growth options CEOs can choose from remain familiar: grow the core, expand into adjacent markets, or build or buy new growth engines. But in just five years, the playbook for capturing growth has changed markedly. Within these three paths are six distinct growth vectors, and as opportunities become more fragmented, CEOs must be more deliberate about how they combine them. They also need to experiment faster and continually reassess where to invest.That’s why each CEO’s Growth Compass will need to establish its own true north, calibrated to growth’s potential contribution to shareholder returns. Not all growth creates value, after all. But its long-term importance is clear: BCG’s analysis of top-quartile S&P 500 performers shows that revenue growth accounts for 49% of total shareholder return over ten years, making it by far the single biggest driver of long-term shareholder value.With that true north established, CEOs can tailor their Growth Compass to their company’s strengths, ambitions, and competitive context, identifying which growth vectors can create more value together than separately. The goal is to build a coordinated, company-wide growth system that can capture emerging opportunities, withstand disruption, and adapt as markets change.

One Growth Compass, Many Combinations
Every Growth Compass starts with six vectors: accelerate the commercial engine, sharpen value and revenue management, capture new demand spaces, expand into new geographies, build new businesses, and finally, pursue acquisitions and partnerships (See Exhibit 1). AI cuts across all six, amplifying their impact while reshaping the competitive dynamics and underlying assumptions about where and how companies can grow.What brings the Growth Compass to life—and makes it unique to each company—is how CEOs use it to chart their own course for growth. By combining mutually reinforcing growth vectors that build on their competitive advantages, companies can create greater value faster than by pursuing any one vector in isolation.

The approach is gaining traction in C-suites. BCG’s analysis of roughly 7,000 third-quarter earnings calls globally found mentions of “multiple growth paths” surging 46.5% quarter over quarter, led by companies in Asia-Pacific. But while the trend is global, there is no universal formula for success. The most promising combination of growth vectors will differ from one company to another, even within the same industry.This is why the starting point for any calibration is determining where a company has a right to win based on its competitive advantages. Crucially, that assessment must also establish where they will be “welcome to win”. Even companies with formidable product advantages risk being shut out of markets if they fail to create value for local economies and stakeholders. And as AI reshapes competition and geopolitical shifts alter market access, both calculations must be continually reassessed.These choices will produce a different Growth Compass for every company, as the following examples illustrate

:Trane Technologies combined expansion into new demand spaces, such as physical AI infrastructure, with acquisitions, partnerships, and commercial scale-up to achieve a five-year annualized TSR of 23%, well above the building products industry median of 5%. Capitalizing on rising demand for data-center cooling and intelligent buildings, the company acquired BrainBox AI to bolster its AI-enabled building-management capabilities and Stellar Energy Digital to expand its modular cooling solutions. By combining these new capabilities with its established HVAC expertise and commercial reach, Trane strengthened its ability to deliver integrated solutions and capture growth opportunities beyond its traditional equipment business.India-based Aurobindo Pharma combined geographic expansion, portfolio diversification, and commercial acceleration to achieve a five-year annualized TSR of 13%, outperforming the pharmaceutical industry median. Leveraging its cost-competitive manufacturing base, the company expanded its European presence through broader product offerings, distribution partnerships, and the acquisition of Ace Laboratories, while investing in complex injectables and differentiated formulations through its Eugia business. Together, these initiatives enabled Aurobindo to bring a wider range of pharmaceutical products to more markets, building on its existing manufacturing and regulatory capabilities.

How CEOs Can Build and Recalibrate Their Growth Compass
As growth opportunities shift, CEOs must continually decide where to commit scarce resources and where to pull back. Pursuing too many opportunities risks spreading resources too thin, while investing in the wrong ones can leave companies exposed as conditions change.To avoid costly miscalculations, CEOs need to build a Growth Compass that guides their investment choices and can be recalibrated as conditions change. The following five steps show how:1. Determine what growth is worth and where you can win.
Just as every company’s Growth Compass is unique, so must be its North Star. For CEOs, that means weighing growth’s potential contribution to TSR against other drivers of shareholder returns and always recognizing that not all growth creates value. Consider that across the S&P 500, revenue growth’s contribution to 10-year TSR between 2015 and 2025 ranged from 123% in real estate to just 34% in utilities and industrials. Over the same period, only 60% of companies achieved value-creating
growth.2

Once CEOs understand growth’s potential contribution to shareholder value, they must look ahead to where new demand and profit pools are emerging. As markets shift, yesterday’s assumptions about where to find growth may no longer hold. CEOs must therefore assess where they have or can build the competitive advantages—including the ability to create value for local economies and stakeholders—needed to capture these opportunities profitably.In consumer markets, for example, longer life spans, changing life milestones, and information overload are reshaping how people live, what they value, and whom they trust. The effects are already evident in the growing pursuit of longevity, the rise of solo living, and consumers' increasing reliance on AI for purchasing advice—creating new opportunities for companies to capture demand beyond traditional product categories. Reacting to shifts in customer expectations can also reveal opportunities to reignite growth in established businesses, as Starbucks is doing by reconnecting with customers (See the sidebar “Starbucks: Reigniting Growth by Reconnecting with Customers”).

Starbucks: Reigniting Growth by Reconnecting with Customers

Starbucks is showing early signs of progress in its turnaround, with a three-year TSR of 12.7% as its “Back to Starbucks” strategy gains traction and lays the foundation for sustainable growth. To reignite growth in its core business, the company has combined investments in customer experience, operational improvements, and a renewed focus on its brand promise. Starbucks invested more than $500 million in staffing and scheduling, introduced new service standards to speed up orders and strengthen customer connections, and redesigned coffeehouses to create more welcoming spaces. These initiatives are beginning to pay off: in Q3 FY2026, US comparable-store sales rose 7.9%, driven by a 4.2% increase in transactions and a 3.6% increase in average ticket.

Whether in consumer or other industries, the goal of this step is the same for every CEO: to establish how much growth should contribute to shareholder value and develop a clear view of where future demand and profit pools are emerging.2. Build a portfolio of mutually reinforcing growth opportunities.
Once CEOs understand where they can win, the next challenge is deciding which growth opportunities to pursue together. The aim is to combine growth vectors that create more value together than separately. That means evaluating opportunities across all six vectors for their potential returns, risks, investment requirements, and strategic fit, with expected contribution to TSR providing a common measure of value. Equally important is understanding where opportunities can reinforce one another by drawing on shared capabilities, customer relationships, technology, or other competitive advantages.AI can make those decisions faster and more informed. AI-enabled diagnostics can help CEOs reassess the economics of growth opportunities and identify promising combinations, while cheaper, faster experimentation, and more sophisticated scenario modeling allow companies to test a wider range of possibilities before committing significant resources.But a portfolio built for growth must also be built for resilience. Traditionally, growth leaders were seen as the visionaries, while risk teams were cast as the buzzkills in the room. In today’s volatile environment, that divide is deeply unproductive. Risk must become an enabler of growth, not simply a constraint on ambition. That means bringing growth and risk leaders together to plan for opportunities and potential disruptions side by side, building strategic buffers into timelines, inventories, and supply chains so companies can sustain ambitious, multiyear investments despite disruption.By the end of this step, CEOs should have a prioritized, resilient portfolio of complementary growth paths, with clear investment commitments and options to pursue as conditions change.3. Organize the enterprise to unlock the full value of growth.
A portfolio of complementary growth opportunities can deliver its full value only if the organization is equipped to execute them together. This is why the CEO must own the Growth Compass, with the CFO ensuring financial discipline while business leaders are accountable for execution.That requires breaking down functional silos so growth initiatives reinforce one another rather than compete for resources. The rise of revenue operations (revops) teams in tech companies demonstrates how integrating sales, marketing, and customer success can strengthen execution across the customer journey. AI can further improve performance through more personalized outreach, faster deal execution, and better pipeline management. Shared data, technology, and performance metrics help align these functions around common growth objectives and measure results.The operating model must also keep pace with the growth strategy. As technology ecosystems diverge, companies face increasingly complex decisions about which technologies they can deploy, where, and under what regulatory constraints. Governance structures built for a more globally integrated world may struggle to accommodate these differences, particularly as geopolitical barriers and restrictions on talent mobility further complicate cross-border operations. CEOs may need to give local businesses greater autonomy, build technology and other capabilities closer to the markets they serve, or forge partnerships where direct expansion is no longer viable.Making this work also requires leaders and employees to embrace a shared growth ambition. Rotating high-potential executives across businesses, disciplines, and geographies can help develop leaders who look beyond their own functions and markets to identify opportunities for collaboration. Without that commitment, even a well-designed Growth Compass risks remaining a strategy on paper.4. Keep pace with how AI changes the economics of growth.
The economics of growth are constantly shifting, as are the assumptions underpinning a company’s Growth Compass. AI, in particular, is changing the cost, speed, and scalability of pursuing growth, making previously unattractive opportunities viable while allowing ambitious challengers to erode established competitive advantages. CEOs must therefore continually reassess which opportunities offer the greatest potential and how these changing economics affect the value of combining different growth vectors.Companies with fewer legacy constraints may be particularly well positioned to capitalize on these shifts, using AI to compete in ways that were previously out of reach. Singapore-based aviation services company SATS, for example, delivered a three-year annualized TSR of 18%, compared to an air freight and logistics industry median of
15%.3

Having acquired Worldwide Flight Services, SATS became a global leader in Air Cargo over that three-year period, effectively tripling its revenue through M&A as well as organic growth in aviation services. SATS has now embarked on an end-to-end AI transformation in its key business processes. What they seek to develop is a new approach to resource planning and operations management in aviation services that will become their new playbook across 225 stations globally. This, in turn, will facilitate standout growth despite manpower constraints in this highly specialized sector.Beyond changing which growth opportunities are viable, AI can also free up resources to pursue them. A BCG analysis of more than 600 US public companies found that among the 6% leading in AI adoption, growth was the dominant source of value creation, with most using productivity gains to expand their businesses rather than simply reduce costs. Between 2022 and 2025, these companies also grew headcount at a compound annual rate three percentage points higher than the median firm in the sample.5. Know when to fix execution and when to rethink strategy.
Knowing when to change course requires CEOs to spot emerging opportunities and threats before they show up in financial results. By connecting external market intelligence with internal business performance, AI can help them identify those shifts earlier. And while CEOs cannot predict black swans (otherwise they wouldn’t exist), AI-enabled scenario planning can help them prepare for potential knock-on effects and respond faster than competitors when disruption strikes.The harder judgment is determining what those signals mean for the growth strategy. When growth falls short of expectations, CEOs must determine whether the problem lies with execution or the strategy itself. If the opportunity remains attractive, the answer may be to fix what’s going wrong and get back on course. If the underlying economics or competitive conditions have changed, however, it may be time to reset the strategy. A temporary drop in sales may warrant an operational response, while sustained market-share losses to an emerging competitor could signal that the company’s growth assumptions no longer hold (See the sidebar “Five Warning Signs That Your Growth Compass Needs a Second Look”).

Five Warning Signs That Your Growth Compass Needs a Second Look 

Customer shifts: Are changing needs or buying behaviors altering demand?  Emerging competitors: Are new entrants, including AI-enabled attackers, taking share?  Regulatory and geopolitical changes: Are new rules or barriers affecting market access?  Economic shifts: Are tariffs, financing costs, inflation, or input prices changing the economics of growth?  Talent shifts: Is the availability or cost of critical skills changing where the company can compete?  

Whether the answer is better execution or a change in strategy, CEOs need continuous visibility into business performance and the ability to make coordinated adjustments to their Growth Compass, rather than waiting for the next annual planning cycle.Having already assessed a portfolio of growth opportunities gives CEOs options without starting from scratch. They can accelerate investments in promising opportunities, pull back from those losing their appeal, or redirect resources as conditions change. As priorities shift, CEOs must also reassess how those growth paths fit together to strengthen the overall growth system.

Disruption will continue to create both risks and opportunities for growth. CEOs cannot control external market conditions, but with a Growth Compass tailored to their company’s strengths and ambitions, they can chart a course to sustainable growth, no matter which way the wind blows.  The authors wish to thank Binh Nguyen, David Gordon, Helen Richmond, and Suman Murthy for their contributions to this article.
